task.question: How many years after retiring following the 2022 Beijing Games did Alysa Liu launch her comeback, per ESPN?
task.evidence: Liu retired after the 2022 Beijing Games only to launch a triumphant comeback two years later.
task.page: Olympic champ Alysa Liu withdraws from figure skating worlds

answer:
Alysa Liu retired after the 2022 Winter Olympics and announced her comeback early in 2023. This means she launched her comeback approximately 1 year after retiring.

FINAL: 1

messages.content: [Cruel Achilles injury has killed the Ben Simmons comeback Australia was dying to see] For the first time in years, Ben Simmons had given us a reason to believe. That's what made the news land so heavily. Because it wasn't just that Simmons had torn his Achilles ; it was that it happened now, days before the NBA season, just as he'd started to answer a question that had followed him for half a decade. Every Achilles tear is cruel, but this one felt slightly more unjust than most. For years, the knock on Simmons was that he didn't care enough. He was supposedly a gifted athlete who'd drifted on talent alone; someone who enjoyed the fruits of the game more than the game itself. This comeback was quietly dismantling that idea. He was returning from back injuries that very well should have been debilitating, which isn't something you just 'talent' your way back from that. So, on the eve of the NBA season, that comeback being cut short by something out of his control was particularly jarring. It robs us of seeing whether the Australian with the greatest peak in the NBA, and someone who had the potential to be an all-time great, could return to that trajectory. Given what Simmons hasn't done on a basketball court in recent years, it's worth reminding ourselves what he was. As a high school player out of Melbourne, he was the first Australian ever selected for the McDonald's All-American game, widely regarded as the premier exhibition in junior basketball in the U.S. He was the consensus No. 1 player in his class, winning the Naismith, Gatorade and Morgan Wootten national player of the year awards. I sat with a then-18-year-old Simmons in the bowels of the United Center in Chicago in April, 2015 during McDonald's All American week. Cameras, recruiters, sneaker reps, and reporters filled every corridor, all waiting on the same handful of teenagers. We sat for an interview on the concourse of the arena. messages.content: [American Alysa Liu, amid comeback bid, leads worlds after short program] BOSTON -- Alysa Liu rarely wavers when it comes to anything, whether it be her abrupt decision to retire after the 2022 Winter Olympics, or the American figure skater's similarly stunning decision to announce her comeback early last year . So when the 19-year-old was pondering what to do for her entrance Wednesday night, when Liu's name was announced for the warm-up to her short program at the world championships, she found herself in a rare situation: She was indecisive. "Then I saw there was a lot of space," Liu said, "and I thought, 'What a great place to do a cartwheel!'" So she cartwheeled, right there on the carpet leading to the ice. And Liu landed it perfectly, just like everything in her program. The result was her international-best of 74.58 points, putting Liu ahead of Mone Chiba of Japan and American teammate Isabeau Levito -- in the midst of her own comeback from an injury -- going into Friday night's free skate. Liu and Levito will be trying to become the first U.S. women's world champion since Kimmie Meissner in 2006. "Moments like these made me realize 16-year-old me was so right. I wouldn't be here if I didn't decide to retire a little bit," said Liu, who was simply burnt out when she stepped away, the sport feeling less like a joy and more like a job back then. "People would tell me not to make the decisions I made," she added, "but I'm really glad. I have good intuition, I think." Chiba scored 73.44 points and Levito scored 73.33. Kaori Sakamoto of Japan was fifth with 71.03 points as she tries to become the first to win four consecutive titles since Carol Heiss in the 1950s and '60s. Two-time defending U.S. champion Amber Glenn, who was among the favorites in Boston, fell on her opening triple axel and was ninth with 67.65.
